strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Clearly identifies and formalizes Instruction-Visual Complexity (IV-Complexity) as a distinct challenge in instruction-based editing with compelling examples

Valuable benchmark contribution: IV-Edit is carefully constructed with ~800 samples, diverse task types (16 types), and rigorous filtering criteria; includes detailed statistics and evaluation protocols

Elegant technical design: Clean separation between VLM-based planning and diffusion execution; training-free attention region injection avoids costly fine-tuning while the five attention rules are well-motivated for preserving global coherence

Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements over strong baselines including proprietary models; particularly strong consistency and overall scores; qualitative results clearly demonstrate superior region localization

Comprehensive experimental validation: Includes meaningful ablations (Table 3 validates reasoning importance), robustness testing against bbox perturbation, and additional comparisons; two-stage GRFO training is sensible
Technical soundness and reproducibility: Properly formulated architecture, detailed appendices with dataset construction, training procedures, and hyperparameters support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Individual components (VLM reasoning, attention manipulation, GRFO) are not novel; contribution is primarily in combination and application rather than fundamental innovation

Evaluation relies entirely on automated metrics: No human evaluation despite this being an image editing task where user perception is critical; Gemini-2.5-Pro ratings have no inter-rater reliability; only 4 evaluation dimensions may not capture full quality

Dataset scale and potential biases: Only ~800 samples is modest for benchmark; heavy dependence on Gemini 2.5 Pro for both data generation and evaluation creates circular dependency; unclear generalization beyond constructed scenarios; task types appear manually selected rather than data-driven

Narrow experimental validation: Only Qwen2.5-VL tested as VLM planner with no ablations using different backbones; GRFO training requires 1K examples but scalability unclear; results may be particularly favorable to Qwen-family models

Method limitations under-discussed: No analysis of error propagation from VLM region proposals; five attention rules lack theoretical justification beyond empirical validation; overlapping bbox handling indicates struggles with complex spatial scenarios

Limited scope for generalization: Benchmark newly proposed with no external validation; results only validated on IV-Edit; unclear how well approach generalizes beyond this specific problem formulation; missing human user studies confirming relevance

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear visual examples of IV-Complexity challenges in instruction-based image editing
Comprehensive and carefully designed IV-Edit benchmark with 800 instruction-image pairs spanning 7 referring types and 16 task types, filling a gap in existing evaluation resources
Practical training-free attention region injection mechanism that enables multi-region edits without additional model training
Thorough experimental evaluation with multiple baselines, detailed ablation studies (Tables 2-3), and extensive qualitative comparisons across diverse scenarios
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective visual illustrations of the problem, architecture, and comparative results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The method primarily assembles existing components (Qwen2.5-VL, MMDiT, GRFO) with straightforward attention mask manipulation; no substantial algorithmic innovation beyond systems engineering

Circular evaluation methodology: IV-Edit is specifically designed for region-aligned editing, creating potential bias toward the proposed approach; no evaluation on existing benchmarks (InpaintImage, GEdit, ImagEdit) to demonstrate generalization
Evaluator bias: Using Gemini-2.5-Pro as the evaluation metric while it generates the benchmark data introduces systematic bias; lacks inter-annotator agreement metrics for manual annotations

Limited generalization evidence: All quantitative results confined to IV-Edit; no evaluation on real user instructions (not LLM-generated); missing human evaluation studies validating that IV-Complexity captures meaningful editing challenges
Unfair experimental comparisons: Training-free RePlan compared against methods trained on massive datasets; ad-hoc weighting scheme for metrics appears designed post-hoc to favor proposed results
Overcomplicated two-stage GRFO training (format learning then planning learning) lacks justification; no clear rationale for this design over end-to-end training
Hand-crafted attention rules (Figure 4) appear heuristically designed without principled justification; no analysis of brittleness or failure modes under distribution shift

Reproducibility concerns: Heavy reliance on proprietary models (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen2.5-VL, Flux.1); complex data construction pipeline scattered across appendices; no clear commitment to releasing code or benchmark

Shallow analysis of why components work: Limited justification for design choices (e.g., simple concatenation in Eq. 2); insufficient analysis of when/why method succeeds or fails; attention discovery in Appendix E disconnected from main narrative
Small-scale RL training: Only ~1K instruction-only examples for GRFO; modest benchmark size (~800 samples) for addressing claimed complexity challenges

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: IV-Complexity identifies genuine limitations in existing instruction-based editing methods, providing valuable framing for the community.

Comprehensive technical approach with thoughtful design choices: The decomposition into reasoning→region-aligned guidance→diffusion execution is well-motivated; the training-free attention injection mechanism is elegant and practical.

Strong empirical validation: Consistent improvements over baselines (Table 1), thorough ablations demonstrating value of reasoning (Table 3) and two-stage RL strategy, robust visual results, and perturbation robustness testing.

Novel benchmark contribution: IV-Edit addresses a real evaluation gap with ~800 carefully filtered samples spanning 7 referring types and 16 task categories, providing infrastructure for future research.
Strong qualitative results: Figures 6, 14-16 consistently demonstrate superior regional localization and reasoning over state-of-the-art baselines.
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Well-organized paper with informative figures explaining the approach and attention mechanisms.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Individual components (VLM reasoning, MMDiT, GRPO) are established techniques; primary contribution is in application/combination rather than fundamental innovation.

Benchmark validation concerns: Modest scale (~800 total samples, ~550 training), no reported inter-annotator agreement statistics, and no human evaluation validating the 5-dimensional automated assessment protocol relying on LLM scoring.

Reproducibility limitations: Code release not mentioned, missing implementation details (hyperparameters, training iterations), heavy reliance on proprietary models (Qwen-VL for planning, Gemini for evaluation).

Limited architectural generalization: All experiments use Flux.1 Kontext backbone; unclear whether attention injection mechanism and VLM reasoning transfer to other diffusion architectures or VLM variants.

Incomplete failure analysis: Limited discussion of when/why the method fails, no analysis of performance scaling with region count, unclear sensitivity to weighting choices in composite evaluation metric.
Narrow experimental scope: Single-image editing only, predefined edit types, no evaluation on non-English instructions or cross-cultural diversity; generalization to compositional scenarios unclear.
Evaluation protocol concerns: Five-point rating scale may be too coarse; no comparison of automated Gemini scores with human judgment; potential evaluation bias when assessing own benchmark.
